757.title: An understanding heart (1 Kings 3:5–9)
757.hook: offered anything, Solomon asks for "an understanding heart", literally a listening heart
757.howItsDone: Jews read Solomon's dream at Gibeon in the book of Kings, among the Former Prophets; some teachers use the Hebrew phrase lev shomea, a listening heart, as a picture of good judgment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David's last words: one who rules justly is like the light of morning. Today a new book, Kings, opens, and a new king is asked a strange question.

"Ask what I shall give thee." That's the whole offer. Solomon, David's son, is newly king, and he has gone to Gibeon to bring offerings. That night, the text says, the LORD appears to him in a dream and speaks those words. No limits, no conditions. In the old wish stories, this is where people ask for gold, or long life, or for their enemies to vanish. Solomon's answer is short and odd. He calls himself a little child who doesn't know how to go out or come in. He has a great people to lead, and he knows he isn't ready. So he asks for one thing.
screen: `A DREAM AT GIBEON.` → `ASK WHAT I SHALL GIVE THEE.` → `I AM BUT A LITTLE CHILD.`

segments.voice: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, Solomon asks for "an understanding heart to judge Thy people." The Hebrew is plainer, and stranger: lev shomea. Lev is heart. Shomea is hearing, the same verb as shema in Deuteronomy's Hear, O Israel. A hearing heart. A listening heart. Notice what he leaves out, because the text lists it: God is pleased that he didn't ask for long life, or riches, or the life of his enemies, but for understanding to discern what is just. And the answer comes back larger than the request: the wisdom, and also the riches and honor he never asked for. Why listening? Solomon's job is to judge, to sit with people's disputes and decide them. A judge can be clever, quick and eloquent, and still never really hear the person in front of him. Some readers point out that in the Hebrew Bible the heart isn't only where feelings live; it's also where a person thinks and decides. So a listening heart is a mind that takes in before it rules. There's humility in it, too. He doesn't ask to be wise. He asks to be able to hear. In this story, wisdom starts with the ears.
screen: `AN UNDERSTANDING HEART.` · `LEV SHOMEA: A HEARING HEART.` · `NOT RICHES, NOT LONG LIFE.` · `WISDOM STARTS WITH THE EARS.` · then, large: `AN UNDERSTANDING HEART TO JUDGE THY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Think of one decision or conversation waiting for you, at work or at home, and before you plan what you'll say, ask what you haven't heard yet: whose side haven't you listened to all the way through? If you pray, you can borrow Solomon's words and ask for an understanding heart; if you don't, just let your listening widen for a minute.

758.title: The two mothers (1 Kings 3:16–28)
758.hook: the true mother gives up her claim to save the child
758.howItsDone: Jews read the judgment of Solomon in the book of Kings, and the passage is assigned as the haftarah, the reading from the Prophets, for the Torah portion Miketz.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon asked for lev shomea. Your line was a listening heart. Today that heart gets its first hard case.

Two women stand before the king, and there is one baby. They live in the same house, and nobody else was there. Each had a son, a few days apart. In the night one baby died, and now each woman says the living child is hers. No witnesses, no records, no way to check. One says, she switched them while I slept. The other says, no, the dead one is yours, the living one is mine. Back and forth, in front of the throne. And the new king, the one who asked for a listening heart, says something that silences the room: bring me a sword.
screen: `TWO WOMEN, ONE LIVING CHILD.` → `NO WITNESSES.` → `BRING ME A SWORD.`

segments.voice: The text calls the two women harlots and never gives their names. They come with no one to speak for them, and the king hears them anyway, in person. First Solomon says both claims back, exactly. He has listened. Then the sword, and the order: divide the living child in two, half to the one and half to the other. Here's the turn. One woman cries out: give her the living child, and don't kill him. The text says she spoke because her compassion was stirred for her son; the Hebrew word is rachamim. The other says, in the 1917 Jewish translation, "It shall be neither mine nor thine; divide it." And the king answers: give the first woman the living child. She is his mother. He didn't find new evidence. He made a moment where love would have to show itself, and it did, as giving way. The real mother was willing to lose the case to save the child. Then the text adds a line about everyone else: all Israel heard of the judgment, and saw that the wisdom of God was in the king, to do justice. Inside the clever lesson sits a hard one. Sometimes the person who is right is the one willing to stop fighting. She didn't win by arguing better. And Solomon's listening heart heard the difference between someone who wanted the child and someone who only wanted to win.

segments.voice: Pick a disagreement you're in right now, a family argument, a fight over credit at work, and ask what's actually at stake underneath: a relationship, a child's peace, a friendship. Hold the two side by side, the win and the child, without deciding anything yet. If you pray, you can ask for the heart to know the difference.

759.title: No sound of iron (1 Kings 6:7)
759.hook: the Temple is built without the sound of hammer or axe
759.howItsDone: Jews read of the Temple's building in the book of Kings, and the Mishnah's teaching about iron and the altar is studied in tractate Middot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two mothers, a sword, and rachamim. Your line was the real mother gives way. Today, the Temple goes up, quietly.

A building site is loud. Saws, drills, a radio, somebody shouting measurements across the lot. One verse in Kings describes a building site of a different kind: Solomon's house for God in Jerusalem. Great stones going up, cedar beams, gold. And in the middle of the description, the text stops for what sounds like an aside. At the site itself, you couldn't hear the hammers. Not because nobody cut stone. Because the cutting happened somewhere else.
screen: `A BUILDING SITE IS LOUD.` → `SOLOMON'S HOUSE FOR GOD.` → `YOU COULDN'T HEAR THE HAMMERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. The house was built of stone made ready before it was brought, and there was "neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building." The Hebrew word for iron is barzel. The cutting happened at the quarry; at the holy place, the stones were only set. Why tell us? The verse doesn't say. But some readers hear an echo from the Torah. In Exodus, an altar of stone is built of stones no tool has been lifted against; lift your tool on it, the text says, and you have profaned it. A later teaching in the Mishnah gives a reason: iron was made to shorten a person's life, and the altar was made to lengthen it, so the thing that shortens shouldn't be raised over the thing that lengthens. And the Talmud tells a legend of the shamir, a tiny creature that could cut stone without any tool, so the work could go on in silence. That one is a story the rabbis tell, not a line in Kings. Side by side, these readings point the same way: the metal that can shorten a life is kept away from the place built to lengthen it. The noise happened offstage, in the quarry. Here there was only placing, fitting, setting. Ordinary life has work like that too: the preparation done out of sight, the kind that's finished before anyone hears it.
screen: `STONE MADE READY AT THE QUARRY.` · `NO TOOL LIFTED ON THE ALTAR.` · `IRON SHORTENS, THE ALTAR LENGTHENS.` · `THE SHAMIR: A LEGEND OF SILENCE.` · then, large: `NEITHER HAMMER NOR AXE NOR ANY TOOL OF IRON.`

segments.voice: Picture one task waiting for you, a sink of dishes, a report, a favor for someone, and see yourself doing it the Temple way: prepared beforehand, done without announcing it or telling anyone how hard it was. Let this quiet minute be the quarry, where you get ready. If you pray, you can offer the work before you begin it.

760.title: Heaven cannot contain thee (1 Kings 8:27)
760.hook: Solomon's dedication prayer admits no house can hold God
760.howItsDone: Jews read Solomon's dedication prayer in the book of Kings, and the Talmud teaches that one who prays should turn toward the land of Israel, toward Jerusalem and the place where the Temple stood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Temple went up in quiet, no barzel heard. Your line was finished before anyone hears it. Today the house is done, and its builder says it isn't big enough.

The building is finished. Cedar walls, gold, the ark carried up into the inner room. Then a cloud fills the house, and the text says the priests couldn't stand to minister because of it. Solomon stands before the altar, in front of the whole gathering of Israel, spreads his hands toward heaven, and begins to pray. It's the moment the whole project was for. And partway through the prayer, he asks a question that seems to undercut the very house he's standing in.
screen: `THE CLOUD FILLS THE HOUSE.` → `HANDS SPREAD TOWARD HEAVEN.` → `A QUESTION IN THE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Will God really dwell on the earth? Solomon answers himself, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain Thee; how much less this house that I have builded!" Heaven of heavens: heaven beyond heaven. The Hebrew word for heaven is shamayim. So at the dedication of the Temple, its builder says the Temple can't hold God. Not even the sky can. Then why build it? The prayer answers in its own way. Again and again, Solomon asks that God's eyes be open toward this house, and that when people pray toward this place, God will hear from heaven. The house isn't a container. It's more like an address: a place to turn toward. Jewish tradition kept that idea after the Temple was gone. The Talmud teaches that someone praying turns toward the land of Israel, toward Jerusalem, toward the place where the house stood. A place can matter deeply and still not hold what it points to. A kitchen where someone you loved used to cook isn't that person, but you might stand in it a little longer than you need to. Solomon builds the house and, in the same breath, refuses to shrink God to fit it.
screen: `WILL GOD DWELL ON THE EARTH?` · `HEAVEN OF HEAVENS CANNOT CONTAIN.` · `NOT A CONTAINER: AN ADDRESS.` · `TURN TOWARD THE PLACE.` · then, large: `HOW MUCH LESS THIS HOUSE THAT I HAVE BUILDED.`

If you pray, you can turn toward a place and still let your prayer be bigger than it; if you don't, just sit with how large the space around you is.

761.title: The foreigner's prayer (1 Kings 8:41–43)
761.hook: Solomon asks that a stranger's prayer in the Temple be heard too
761.howItsDone: Jews read Solomon's prayer for the foreigner in the book of Kings alongside the Torah's command to care for the stranger, and commentators such as Rashi ask why the foreigner's prayer is to be answered in full.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon said no house could hold God. Your line was a place to turn toward. Today, in the same prayer, he makes room for someone outside his people.

Somebody arrives from far away. Different clothes, a different accent, maybe a different language. They've heard about this place and walked a long road to reach it. Now they stand in the courtyard among people who know the customs, and they don't. They pray anyway. Who is that prayer for? Will anyone listen? Solomon's dedication prayer, in the middle of asking for his own people, stops to answer exactly that.
screen: `SOMEBODY FROM FAR AWAY.` → `A LONG ROAD TO GET HERE.` → `WHO HEARS THEIR PRAYER?`

segments.voice: Solomon has prayed for Israel in defeat, in drought, in famine and plague. Then he turns to the foreigner, in Hebrew the nochri, who is not of Israel but comes out of a far country for the sake of God's name, having heard, the text says, of God's great name, strong hand and outstretched arm. When this stranger prays toward this house, Solomon asks, hear in heaven, and do according to all that the stranger calls to you for, so that all the peoples of the earth may know God's name. Later readers noticed a detail. For Israel, Solomon asks God to give each person according to their ways, since God knows the heart. For the foreigner, he asks God to do according to all they call for. The commentator Rashi reads that difference as care. Someone of Israel knows the relationship and can bear an answer of no. But a foreigner who is turned away might say, I came all this way to that house, and I wasn't heard. So, Rashi says, Solomon asked that the stranger be answered in full. Later, the prophet Isaiah speaks of God's house as a house of prayer for all peoples. And the Torah tells Israel to care for the stranger, because they were strangers in the land of Egypt. The house is built by one people, and it is open to another's voice.
screen: `NOCHRI: THE FOREIGNER.` · `DO ALL THAT THE STRANGER ASKS.` · `RASHI: SO NO ONE GOES HOME UNHEARD.` · `A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL PEOPLES.`

762.title: The Queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10)
762.hook: she comes with hard questions and says "the half was not told me"
762.howItsDone: Jews read the visit of the queen of Sheba in the book of Kings, and the same visit is told again in the second book of Chronicles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon prayed for the nochri, the foreigner. Your line was hear the stranger too. Today a foreigner does arrive, and she isn't coming to pray. She's coming to test.

A caravan comes up the road to Jerusalem: camels loaded with spices, gold and precious stones. At its head is the queen of Sheba. She has heard of Solomon's fame, and she doesn't take it on faith. The 1917 Jewish translation puts it bluntly: she came "to prove him with hard questions." She isn't here to admire. She's here to check. And by the end of her visit she'll say a line that turns her doubt inside out.
screen: `A CARAVAN TO JERUSALEM.` → `SHE HEARD THE FAME.` → `SHE CAME TO TEST HIM.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew word for her hard questions is chidot, riddles, the same word used for Samson's riddle in the book of Judges. She comes with puzzles that test a mind. She speaks with him of all that was in her heart, and Solomon answers every question; nothing was hidden from the king that he could not tell her. Then she looks around: the house he built, the food on his table, his servants and how they're dressed, the offerings he brings up. And she says, in the 1917 Jewish translation, "I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it; and, behold, the half was not told me." Look at how she learns. She doesn't settle for reports; she travels to see. She brings her hardest questions, not her easiest. And when the reality is bigger than the rumor, she says so out loud, with no embarrassment about having doubted. She also blesses Solomon's God, and says God made him king to do justice and righteousness. Then she gives her gifts, receives his, and goes home to her own land. The text never gives her a name. Later traditions tell more stories about her; Kings tells only this visit. A short scene, and a way of learning: doubt enough to go and look, ask what you actually want to know, and be honest when you find more than you were told.

763.howItsDone: Jews read Solomon's later years in the book of Kings, and the Talmud uses his story to show why the Torah's limits on a king matter even for the wise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a queen came with chidot, hard questions. Your line was the half was not told. Today, the end of Solomon's story, and it turns.

A heart that hears. That's what Solomon asked for in a dream, at the very start. Since then he has judged between two mothers, built a house in quiet, prayed, saying heaven itself can't hold God, and asked that strangers be heard. A queen came to test him and went home amazed. Then the text turns a page and writes a sentence that begins, when Solomon was old. There's no single scene of falling. It's slower than that.
screen: `A HEART THAT HEARS.` → `JUDGE, BUILDER, PRAYER.` → `WHEN SOLOMON WAS OLD.`

segments.voice: The text says Solomon loved many foreign women, and gives the number itself: seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines. The Torah had warned that a king must not multiply wives, so that his heart not turn away. And verse four says just that, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods." He built high places for the gods of his wives' peoples, on the hill before Jerusalem. But the text doesn't let this be anyone else's fault. The LORD is angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned. His heart, the verse goes on, was not whole, in Hebrew not shalem, with God, as David's heart had been. The Talmud tells that Solomon reasoned he could take many wives and not be turned, and he was. His story opens with a heart, lev shomea, a listening heart. It closes with a heart that turned. Same heart. And there's no single moment of turning: the text lists marriages, then shrines for the gods of his wives, one after another. Nobody in the story wakes up one morning a different person. Many readers take Solomon's drift as a warning. The story doesn't call wisdom worthless; it shows that wisdom alone didn't keep him from turning. A king given wisdom in a dream still needed to keep choosing, every year, into old age. And the cost comes due in the next generation.
screen: `THE TORAH'S WARNING TO KINGS.` · `HIS HEART WAS NOT SHALEM.` · `A LISTENING HEART THAT TURNED.` · `ONE SMALL CHOICE, THEN ANOTHER.` · then, large: `WHEN SOLOMON WAS OLD.`

segments.voice: Is there something that matters to you that has slowly slipped, a habit of prayer, a friendship you used to tend, a value you once held tightly? With no scolding, trace it back to the small choice where the drift started, then name one small choice that could turn you back toward it. If you pray, you can ask for a whole heart.
Shalem. The Hebrew word for whole, the wholeness Solomon's heart lost toward God as he grew old. Today's word.

Your line: one small choice at a time. The week in lines: a listening heart, the real mother gives way, finished before anyone hears it, a place to turn toward, hear the stranger too, the half was not told, and this one. Day seven hundred sixty-three.

chat.says: How could someone as wise as Solomon end up turning away?
options: Wisdom alone didn't keep him; his heart turned slowly, one choice at a time.
A foreign army forced him to build the shrines against his will.
The prophets told him to build the shrines, to keep peace with his neighbors.
chat.meaning: The text names no single moment: when Solomon was old, his heart was not shalem, whole, after choice upon choice. Wisdom alone didn't keep him.
